title: Fluorine-19 Imaging and Spectroscopy
summary: 19F is spin 1/2 at 100 percent natural abundance with a gyromagnetic ratio of 40.078 MHz/T, 94.1 percent of 1H, so per nucleus it carries 83 percent of the 1H sensitivity and is the second most favourable nucleus in the table. Mobile 19F in tissue is effectively zero, so every image is a background-free hot spot and every signal is something you injected: a perfluorocarbon label on cells, an oxygen reporter whose R1 reads pO2, a fluorinated drug, or an inhaled anaesthetic. The costs are all on the other side. The organofluorine shift range exceeds 350 ppm, so multi-line agents give chemical shift displacement measured in whole pixels; the 1H and 19F frequencies differ by only 5.9 percent, which makes dual-tuned coils and trap isolation awkward; and detection limits sit in the high micromolar to millimolar range, seven or more orders of magnitude above what 18F PET sees with the same element.

facts.label: Nucleus properties
facts.value: Spin 1/2, 100 percent natural abundance, 40.078 MHz/T, which is 94.1 percent of the 1H gyromagnetic ratio; receptivity 0.83 relative to 1H. Larmor 60.1 MHz at 1.5T, 120.2 MHz at 3T, 280.5 MHz at 7T
facts.note: The 0.83 is (gamma_F/gamma_H)^3 at equal spin density; the real deficit in vivo is concentration, since you are working at mM against roughly 80 M of 1H in tissue water.

facts.label: Frequency separation from 1H
facts.value: 5.9 percent, which is 3.8 MHz at 1.5T, 7.5 MHz at 3T and 17.5 MHz at 7T
facts.note: Too close for the trap and PIN-diode isolation that works for 13C or 31P at a quarter or a third of the 1H frequency, so dual-tuned 1H/19F coils usually trade efficiency on one channel or switch a single structure between the two.

facts.label: Biological 19F background
facts.value: Effectively zero for liquid-state sequences. Total body fluorine is of order a few grams, over 99 percent bound as fluorapatite in bone and teeth with a rigid-lattice T2 of tens of microseconds; plasma fluoride sits near 1 micromolar
facts.note: This is the whole selling point: no partial volume from an endogenous pool, no water suppression, no baseline. It survives only while your TE is long enough to have lost the solid-state signal.

facts.label: Chemical shift range
facts.value: Organofluorine spans more than 350 ppm, roughly +50 to -300 ppm versus CFCl3 at 0 ppm, and over 800 ppm if inorganic fluorides are included. 300 ppm is 36 kHz at 3T and 84 kHz at 7T
facts.note: Excellent for resolving a drug from its metabolites, terrible for imaging: no clinical transmit chain excites 36 kHz uniformly, so agents are chosen for having one line rather than for chemistry.

facts.label: 19F payload of common agents
facts.value: Neat perfluoro-15-crown-5-ether (PFCE) is about 61 M in 19F with 20 equivalent nuclei on one line near -92 ppm. Perflubron (PFOB) is about 66 M total but splits 17 nuclei over five or six lines, only 3 of them in the CF3. Hexafluorobenzene is about 52 M in 6 equivalent nuclei. PFPE carries more than 40 nuclei, PERFECTA 36 equivalent nuclei
facts.note: What matters is not fluorine content but chemically equivalent fluorine content: imaging the PFOB CF3 line throws away 82 percent of the fluorine you injected.

facts.label: Detection limit in 19F concentration, 3T
facts.value: 11.8 +/- 3.0 mM for PFCE at 24 C rising to 379.9 +/- 51.8 mM for PFOB at 37 C, for sequences optimised per agent
facts.note: The 30-fold spread across agents and temperature is the single most useful number in the field; it is why PFCE and PFPE dominate cell labelling and why PFOB persists mainly for its clinical safety record.

facts.label: Cell tracking sensitivity
facts.value: About 10^5 cells per voxel at 3T in under 10 min, from the clinical dendritic cell vaccine trial; labelling densities of 7.9 x 10^11 19F per macrophage to 3.7 x 10^12 19F per dendritic cell. That is of order 10^17 19F nuclei per detectable voxel
facts.note: In that trial the apparent cell number at the intradermal injection site fell by about 50 percent at 24 h, which is a delivery and retention measurement rather than a viability measurement.

facts.label: PFC relaxation times
facts.value: T1 of most fluorinated agents lies between 1 and 4 s, and useful imaging requires T2 above about 10 ms; PFCE and PFPE sit comfortably in that window while polymer probes often do not
facts.note: Long T1 makes 19F a TR-limited experiment, so the practical gains come from Ernst-angle steady state, bSSFP and RARE rather than from more averages at a long TR.

facts.label: Tumour pO2 by 19F, hexafluorobenzene
facts.value: Dunning prostate R3327-AT1 at 4.7T: central regions 1.4 to 6.4 mmHg, peripheral regions 7.9 to 78.9 mmHg, with stability about +/-2 mmHg over 20 min; carbogen or 100 percent O2 moved the periphery significantly but not the centre
facts.note: The centre-to-periphery gradient of more than an order of magnitude is the point; a single whole-tumour pO2 number is close to meaningless.

facts.label: Oximetry calibration and precision
facts.value: R1 = A + B x pO2, linear over the physiological range, with A and B both temperature dependent. For FC-43 at 37 C a 5 percent error in T1 gives about +/-10 torr (40 percent) at pO2 = 25 torr and about +/-16 torr (11 percent) at pO2 = 150 torr
facts.note: The mechanism is collisional relaxation by dissolved paramagnetic O2, so the probe reports the pO2 of the fluid it sits in, and the fractional precision is worst exactly where radiobiology cares most, in the hypoxic range.

facts.label: 5-FU pharmacokinetics in human liver
facts.value: 5-FU clears from liver within 17 to 26 min after bolus; the catabolite FBAL plateaus at 1.0 +/- 0.2 mM at 60 +/- 10 min, about 20 percent of the injected dose, with FBAL T1 of 1.6 +/- 0.2 s at 1.5T. Localised 3D CSI of both at 1.5T runs at about 4 min per time point
facts.note: Spectral layout: FBAL is about 19 ppm from 5-FU, which is 1.1 kHz at 1.5T and 2.3 kHz at 3T; the fluoronucleotides sit 4.5 to 5 ppm and the fluoronucleosides 3.5 to 3.8 ppm from 5-FU, and both of those shifts are pH dependent.

facts.label: Fluorinated psychiatric drugs in brain
facts.value: Steady-state whole-brain concentrations of 12 +/- 5 micromolar for fluvoxamine and 13 +/- 6 micromolar for combined fluoxetine plus norfluoxetine, with brain-to-plasma ratios near 10. Brain elimination half-life 58 h for fluvoxamine against 26 h in plasma; 382 +/- 48 h for fluoxetine plus norfluoxetine. R-fluoxetine at 80 and 120 mg/day reached 34.9 and 41.4 micromolar in brain at 5 weeks against 25.5 micromolar for the racemate
facts.note: Micromolar detection is only possible because these are unlocalised or coarsely localised whole-head acquisitions over tens of minutes; there is no spatial information worth the name at these concentrations.

facts.label: Inhaled anaesthetic washout, human head
facts.value: Isoflurane elimination from the head is biexponential with decay half-times of 9.5 min and 130 min
facts.note: The signal was too weak with a surface receive coil to assign the two compartments to specific tissue, so the identification of the fast compartment with brain is an assumption borrowed from perfusion-limited pharmacokinetic models.

facts.label: Why 18F PET is a different experiment
facts.value: A 370 MBq 18F-FDG dose is about 6 picomoles of 18F in the entire patient, and 18F has a 109.8 min half-life and decays by positron emission. A 19F MR experiment needs roughly 0.1 to 10 mM of 19F in the voxel, of order a micromole per millilitre
facts.note: Same element, different isotope, and a sensitivity gap of six to nine orders of magnitude: 18F is invisible to MR and 19F carries no radiation dose, no half-life and no cyclotron.

practice: Shim and localise on 1H through the body coil, then switch to 19F without moving anything. A singly tuned 19F coil produces no anatomical image at all, so your overlay is only as good as the assumption that the subject did not move between the two acquisitions.

Put a sealed external reference of known 19F content in the field of view on every scan and measure its T1 separately. 19F signal is proportional to the number of nuclei, which is what makes absolute quantification possible, but only against a reference that saw the same B1 and the same saturation.

Calibrate transmit at the 19F frequency itself rather than scaling the 1H reference voltage. A dual-tuned coil has different efficiency and different loading at 120.2 MHz and 127.7 MHz, and the error goes straight into any flip-angle-dependent quantification.

Choose readout bandwidth from the chemical shift you must live with: displacement in pixels is the shift in Hz divided by the Hz per pixel. The roughly 40 ppm between the PFOB CF3 and the chain CF2 envelope is about 4.8 kHz at 3T, so sub-pixel displacement would need an absurd bandwidth. Use spectrally selective excitation or a multi-peak model-based reconstruction instead.

Measure T1 of your agent in the condition you will actually image, meaning the cell type, the temperature and the oxygenation, then set TR and flip angle from that. Optimising on a room-temperature phantom is defensible: the reported efficiency loss from using the wrong condition is bounded at about 13 percent.

Quantify in moles of 19F first and convert to cells afterwards, using a 19F per cell figure measured by high-resolution NMR on a pellet from the same labelling batch. Labelling efficiency varies by cell type across more than an order of magnitude.

For oximetry, recalibrate R1 against pO2 for your own probe batch at your field and at 37 C, and measure temperature independently. Slope and intercept both fall as temperature rises, so a thermal drift reads as an oxygenation change.
pitfalls: PTFE and other fluoropolymers in coil formers, cable jackets, connectors, table padding and lubricants carry solid-state 19F with T2 of tens of microseconds. A conventional TE never sees it, but UTE and ZTE sequences pull it back as a broad hump that rolls the baseline and corrupts quantification.

The 5.9 percent 1H to 19F separation defeats ordinary trap isolation. Dual-tuned coils leak 1H into the 19F channel or lose efficiency at one frequency, so always benchmark the dual-tuned coil against a single-tuned 19F coil on the same phantom before you believe a sensitivity claim.

Multi-resonance agents give you both problems at once: chemical shift displacement of each line into a different pixel, and a divided signal that no single excitation recovers. Picking a one-line agent at the outset is cheaper than fixing it in reconstruction.

PFC relaxation times are not a property of the molecule alone. T1 depends on pO2 and temperature, and shifts again once the agent is internalised into cells or a lipid environment, so an oximetry calibration and a T1-weighted quantification can silently contradict each other.

19F intensity counts fluorine nuclei, not live cells. When a labelled cell dies the perfluorocarbon is scavenged by resident macrophages and the hot spot stays where it was, so longitudinal cell counts are biased upward and never show clearance that has actually happened.

Treating 18F PET results and 19F MR results as the same measurement. PET reports sub-nanomolar tracer distribution with a 110 min clock; 19F MR reports millimolar chemical distribution with no clock at all, and the two cannot be cross-calibrated.
